This book is not “world geography” — it is **Eritrea**. Outcomes: read the land’s story (rocks), water, climate, plants and animals, soils, how people make a living, and who lives where.

cards.title: 2.1 What is Hydrological Cycle
body: **A hydrological cycle** is the movement of water between the atmosphere, the land, and the sea.

cards.title: Hydrological cycle
body: Rain is the recharge. In Eritrea most rain is summer; much of it evaporates again before it can be stored.

cards.title: The water cycle in five steps
body: **1. Evaporation** from oceans, lakes, rivers and wet ground, and **transpiration** from plants, put water vapour into the air.
**2. Condensation:** rising vapour cools and forms clouds. **3. Precipitation:** water falls back as rain (or hail).

**4. Infiltration and percolation:** part of the rain soaks into the soil and down into rocks to become groundwater. **5. Runoff:** the rest flows over the surface into streams, rivers and the sea, and the cycle repeats. The study of water on the earth's surface is called **hydrology**.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Zone of Aeration
body: Most of the time the pore spaces contain air and water.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Zone of Saturation
body: The amount of water this zone holds depends on the permeability of rocks.
Permeable rocks allow water to pass through them, while impermeable rocks do not allow water to pass through them.
A well dug into the zone of saturation fills with water up to the level of the water table.
When water is taken from the well faster than it can flow in from saturated rock, the water table sinks.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Zone of Confined Water
body: The most common aquifer is made of unconsolidated sand and gravel.
Often, there are layers of impermeable rocks that exclude water.
If a well is drilled from the surface down into the aquifer, the pressure will force water to rise in the well.
If the pressure is sufficient to force the water to the surface without artificial pumping, the free flow that results is called an **artesian well**.

cards.title: Three groundwater zones
body: **Zone of aeration** (top): pore spaces hold both air and water; moisture varies.

**Zone of saturation:** every pore and crack is full of water – the source of wells and springs. Its top is the **water table**, which lies closer to the surface in valleys than under hills, so wells are cheaper to dig in valley bottoms. Pumping faster than water flows in makes the water table sink.

**Zone of confined water:** a permeable **aquifer** (often sand and gravel) lies between impermeable **aquicludes**. A well drilled into it rises under pressure: an **artesian well** flows to the surface by itself; a **sub-artesian well** rises only part of the way.

lessons.title: Distribution of Water Resource in Eritrea

cards.title: 2.3.1 Surface Water Resources
body: The pattern of rainfall in Eritrea is erratic in nature.
The average annual rainfall in the Highlands varies from 500mm to 700mm.
In the Lowlands, the amount of rainfall is much lower, while evapo-transpiration is higher than in the Highlands.
The high rates of evapo-transpiration and irregular rainfall have made surface water unreliable for such activities like irrigation and hydroelectric power.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Ground Water Resources in Eritrea
body: Water resource potential in Eritrea is not well-known since no systematic study has been carried out.
A large supply of ground water is available in areas adjacent to wet areas or flood plains.

The degree to which water runs off or percolates into the ground depends on factors such as the soil texture, the types of rocks, the vegetation cover, the degree of slopes and the amount of rainfall.
The largest part of the lava plateau is found around Senafe.

cards.title: 2.4 Water Resource Zones of Eritrea
body: Based on relief, rainfall, surface water and ground water, the water resources in Eritrea are divided into three major regions.
The evapo-transpiration rate is about 1700mm/year.
The recharge rate of the ground water is estimated to be 50 to 150mm/ year.
Springs, hand dug wells, and manmade dams are commonly found in the highlands.
The depth of ground water ranges from 7m to 150m.

cards.title: Comparing the three water-resource zones
body: **Highlands** (1,500–3,013 m): rain 500–700 mm, PET about 1,700 mm, groundwater 7–150 m deep. Problems: over-pumping for irrigation and siltation of dams. Development: dug wells, boreholes, river diversion, small dams and cisterns.

**Western lowlands and escarpments** (500–1,500 m): rain 200–500 mm (over 1,000 mm on the Green Belt), seasonal rivers (Anseba, Barka, Mereb-Gash), groundwater 5–100 m. Problems: low recharge, saline water, siltation, high PET. Development: hand-dug wells, sub-surface dams, drilling, river diversion.

**Eastern lowlands** (below 500 m): rain under 200 mm, PET over 1,900 mm, groundwater only 3–7 m deep, recharged mainly by floods from the highlands. Problems: low rain and recharge, saline water. Development: hand-dug wells and sub-surface dams in sandy river beds, boreholes outside river courses.

cards.title: 2.5 Water Conservation in Eritrea
body: In some parts of the country, rural residents have to walk a long distance to sources of water because water supply infrastructure is not well developed.
Water conservation or a wise use of water is, therefore, essential.
Measures of water conservation are practiced because they (a) prevent or minimize siltation of surface-water reservoirs.
Terraces check erosion and help water to sink and enrich the ground water.
In Eritrea, ground water has a long history, but it has not been fully utilized.

cards.title: Aquifer
body: Rock or sediment that stores and yields water. Texture, slope, vegetation and rainfall decide how good it is.

cards.title: Groundwater layers
body: **Surface water:** seasonal rivers (wadis) — Setit, Mereb-Gash, Barka, Anseba and short Red Sea catchments. Unreliable for big irrigation or hydropower because rain is low and jumpy.

**Problems:** siltation, salinity, high evapotranspiration, weak recharge. **Fixes:** terraces, dams and ponds (Gerset, Fanko), river diversion, boreholes, hand-dug wells, sub-surface dams in sandy wadis, don’t contaminate what you have.

tips.text: Summer rains are the major source of water in Eritrea.
Low and irregular rainfall makes surface water unreliable for economic activities like irrigation and hydroelectric power.
How ever, a large supply of ground water is available in places adjacent to wet areas.

There is also a large potential for ground water, but its economic utility is affected by several factors including soil texture, types of rocks, vegetation cover, degree of slopes and amount of rainfall.

The major problems associated with water resources are siltation, high level of salinity, high evapotranspiration and low rainfall and recharge rates. Such problems can be tackled through constructing river diversions, drilling boreholes, and hand-dug wells.

Since rainwater is the source for both surface and ground water, it has to be conserved for use during dry season. In addition, water should be properly utilized in order to protect it from contamination and maximize its utility.
Furthermore, smallscale water developments like ponds are highly recommended to conserve water for drinking and irrigation purposes.

questions.label: 20. Which practice best conserves water in Eritrea's dry areas?

similar.a: It delivers water directly to roots with little evaporation.

options.B: Building micro-dams and ponds to store runoff

why: Answer B: Building micro-dams and ponds to store runoff
Rain falls in a short season and quickly runs off.
Micro-dams and ponds store this water for the dry season.
The other actions reduce stored water.
questions.tip: Separate surface water (rivers, dams) from groundwater (aquifers, wells, springs) and link each water zone to rainfall and relief.
